text: I am sick of my life. I will let my complaint run free; I will speak out of the bitterness of my soul.
I will say to God: Do not condemn me. Tell me what charge you bring against me.
Does it please you to oppress me, to spurn the work of your own hands while you smile on the schemes of the wicked?
Do you have eyes of flesh? Do you see as a mortal sees?
Are your days like the days of a mortal, your years like the years of a man,
that you must search out my guilt and hunt for my sin—
though you know that I am not guilty, and no one can rescue me from your hand?
Your hands shaped me and made me, every part of me; will you now turn and destroy me?

versions.text: Your hands shaped me and made me; will you now turn and destroy me?
versions.explanation: The Hebrew phrase יַחַד סָבִיב ("altogether, all around") is left untranslated. Adding "every part of me" restores the sense that God formed the whole of Job, which sharpens the contrast with "destroy me," and it keeps the line short enough for oral reading.

text: Remember, I pray, that you molded me like clay. Will you return me to the dust?

versions.text: Remember that you molded me like clay. Will you return me to the dust?
versions.explanation: The particle נָא softens the imperative into an entreaty ("remember, please"). Including it conveys Job's pleading tone rather than a bare command, and the added phrase gives the line a fuller cadence when spoken.

text: Did you not pour me out like milk and curdle me like cheese,
clothe me with skin and flesh, and knit me together with bones and sinews?
You granted me life and showed me mercy, and your care watched over my spirit.
Yet this is what you hid in your heart; now I know what you had in mind.
If I sinned, you were watching me, and you would not let my guilt go unpunished.
If I am guilty—woe to me! And even if I am innocent, I cannot lift up my head, for I am filled with shame and see nothing but my affliction.

versions.text: If I am guilty—woe to me! And even if I am innocent, I cannot lift up my head, for I am filled with shame and drowned in my affliction.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew has a form of רָאָה ("to see/look upon") — Job is "sated with shame and looking on my affliction." "Drowned in" introduces an image (drowning) that is not in the text; "see nothing but my affliction" keeps the seeing imagery while remaining natural for reading aloud.

text: If I hold my head high, you hunt me like a lion and display your power against me again and again.
You bring fresh witnesses against me and pour out your anger on me; wave after wave assaults me.
Why then did you bring me out of the womb? I wish I had died before any eye saw me,
that I had never come to be—carried straight from the womb to the grave.
Are not my days few? Let me alone, turn away from me, so I may have a moment's comfort
before I go, never to return, to the land of darkness and deepest shadow,
to a land of gloom, dark as night itself, of deathly shadow and no order, where even the light is like darkness.

versions.text: to the land of gloom and chaos, where even the light is like darkness.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew piles up three terms — עֵיפָתָה (gloom), אֹפֶל (thick darkness), צַלְמָוֶת (deathly shadow) — before "and no order." The current rendering drops צַלְמָוֶת entirely, flattening the verse's cumulative effect; restoring it preserves the content and the rhythmic build of the closing line.

versions.text: to the land of deep gloom and darkest shadow, a land without order, where even the light is like darkness.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew has an explicit simile in the first clause — עֵיפָתָה כְּמוֹ אֹפֶל, "gloom like thick darkness" — which the current rendering absorbs into the adjective "deep," leaving the comparison unexpressed. Restoring the simile preserves the deliberate doubling of the like-darkness image (it recurs at the end of the verse) and keeps the three-fold pile-up of gloom, shadow and disorder that gives the closing line its build. The current reading is not wrong in sense, only compressed.
